items.front: Article 368 — where can an amendment bill start, and is President's assent optional?
items.back: In either House of Parliament (no state legislature, no President's prior recommendation). Since the 24th Amendment (1971), President's assent is mandatory.
items.examPoint: Amendment bill introduced only in Parliament (not state legislatures); 24th Amendment made President's assent mandatory

items.front: Three routes to amend the Constitution?
items.back: Simple majority (outside Art 368), special majority, and special majority + ratification by half the states.
items.examPoint: Three routes — simple majority, special majority, special majority + ratification by half the states

items.back: Majority of the total membership of each House PLUS two-thirds of the members present and voting. No joint sitting for amendment bills.
items.examPoint: Special majority — 50% of total membership + two-thirds of members present and voting

items.front: Which amendment added the Ninth Schedule, and under which PM?
items.back: The 1st Amendment (1951), under PM Jawaharlal Nehru — to protect land-reform laws (Art 31B).
items.examPoint: 1st Amendment 1951 — added Ninth Schedule and Articles 31A & 31B

items.front: Can a Ninth Schedule law be examined by the courts?
items.back: Yes — post I.R. Coelho (2007), laws added after 24 April 1973 are open to basic-structure review. Parliament CAN place a law in the Ninth Schedule.
items.examPoint: I.R. Coelho (2007) — Ninth Schedule laws post-24 April 1973 open to judicial review; elements of basic structure

items.front: Is the 'basic structure' defined in the Constitution?
items.back: No — it is a judge-made, open-ended doctrine from Kesavananda Bharati (1973); the Constitution does not define it.
items.examPoint: Basic Structure Doctrine — Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), 13-judge bench

items.front: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) — bench size and core ruling?
items.back: 13-judge bench (largest ever); Parliament can amend any part but cannot destroy the 'basic structure'. Overruled Golaknath.
items.examPoint: Basic Structure Doctrine — Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), 13-judge bench

items.front: Amendability of FRs — Shankari Prasad → Golaknath → Kesavananda?
items.back: Shankari Prasad (1951)/Sajjan Singh (1965): FRs amendable → Golaknath (1967): not amendable → Kesavananda (1973): amendable but not the basic structure.
items.examPoint: Shankari Prasad (1951) & Golaknath (1967) — evolving view on amendability of Fundamental Rights

items.front: Which case FIRST struck down a constitutional provision using the basic-structure test?
items.back: Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) — the 39th Amendment clause placing the PM's election beyond judicial review was void (free & fair elections).
items.examPoint: Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) — 39th Amendment clause on PM's election struck as violating basic structure (free & fair elections)
items.source: UPSC 2019 PYQ; Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)

items.front: Minerva Mills (1980) — what did it hold?
items.back: Struck down 42nd Amendment clauses (Art 368 (4) & (5)); limited amending power and judicial review are part of the basic structure.
items.examPoint: Minerva Mills (1980) & Waman Rao (1981) — limits on amending power; judicial review as a basic feature

items.back: 42nd (1976) 'Mini-Constitution' added Socialist/Secular/Integrity + Fundamental Duties; 44th (1978) made Right to Property a legal right (Art 300A) and shielded Arts 20 & 21.
items.examPoint: 42nd Amendment 1976 ('Mini-Constitution') — Socialist/Secular/Integrity, Fundamental Duties, Part IVA

items.back: 103rd (2019) 10% EWS; 105th (2021) states identify SEBCs; 106th (2023) one-third women's reservation (latest as of 2026).
items.examPoint: 106th Amendment 2023 — Women's Reservation (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam), one-third of seats

items.front: Which amendment gave GST, and which lowered the voting age?
items.back: 101st Amendment (2016) = GST; 61st Amendment (1989) lowered the voting age 21 to 18.
items.examPoint: 61st Amendment 1989 — voting age reduced from 21 to 18

items.front: Must a federal-provision amendment be ratified by ALL states?
items.back: No — ratification by at least half (≥50%) of the state legislatures suffices; the amendment idea was borrowed from South Africa.
items.examPoint: Special majority + ratification by at least half the state legislatures (federal provisions)
